title: Cannabis Balms, Lotions, Tinctures and RSO Compared
h1: Cannabis Wellness Products Compared: Balms, Lotions, Tinctures and RSO
metaDescription: Cannabis balms, lotions, tinctures and RSO compared: how each is used, how fast it acts, how to measure a dose and what label ratios like 1:1 actually mean.
excerpt: Balms, lotions, tinctures and RSO often get grouped together, but they work very differently. Here's how each is used, how fast it acts and how to read its label.
keyTakeaways: Balms and standard lotions work locally on the skin; transdermal products are designed to carry cannabinoids into the bloodstream.
Tincture drops held under the tongue absorb partly through the mouth lining, yet much of the liquid is swallowed and behaves like an edible.
RSO is a full-extract oil that can hold hundreds of milligrams of THC per gram, so servings are tiny.
A ratio such as 1:1 shows the balance of CBD to THC; the milligrams per serving show the dose.

body:
Balms, lotions, tinctures and RSO are often sold as cannabis wellness products, a marketing label rather than a promise. None of them is smoked, but they differ in how they enter your body, how fast they act and how precisely you can measure them. Here's a plain comparison to help you read each label.

## What “cannabis wellness products” usually means

People choose these formats for practical reasons: no smoke, a measured dose in milligrams, or a topical for one spot without feeling high. None of that makes them health products. None of them is an approved medicine, and research on these consumer formats is limited. Talk with your clinician before using them for a health reason, especially if you're pregnant or take medications.

## Balms and salves: concentrated, for one spot

Balms and salves are thick, waxy topicals made to stay where you rub them in. A CBD balm and a THC balm work the same basic way. Cannabinoids are very fat-soluble, which lets them enter the skin's outer layer but makes it hard to go deeper. A review of skin-delivery research found that CBD tends to collect in that outer layer. In one small German experiment, THC salves applied for three days left no detectable THC in three volunteers' blood or urine. Our [guide to cannabis topicals](/blog/guide-to-cannabis-topicals/) covers every type.

## Lotions, including transdermal formulas

Lotions spread easily over larger areas, and a regular cannabis lotion works on and in the skin, much like a balm.

Transdermal products are different. A patch, gel or transdermal cannabis lotion uses special carriers to push cannabinoids past the skin's outer barrier and into your bloodstream. So a THC transdermal can act on your whole body. The same route can also keep blood levels steady over many hours. In Michigan, non-oral THC products such as transdermal patches can hold as much as 100 mg of THC per dose. If the label doesn't say transdermal, assume it's a topical.

## Tinctures: dropper doses under the tongue or in food

A tincture is a liquid extract in alcohol or oil, sold with a dropper that's often marked in milliliters, so you can measure small, repeatable amounts. Held under the tongue, some of a THC tincture absorbs through the lining of the mouth. Much of it still gets swallowed, though, and that part acts like an edible. Swallowed cannabis usually takes effect within two hours, sometimes in as little as 30 minutes, and full effects can take up to four hours. For adult-use tinctures, Michigan allows no more than 10 mg of THC in a dose and 200 mg in a container. Our [cannabis tincture guide](/blog/cannabis-tincture-guide/) walks through dropper math.

## RSO: a whole-plant oil that calls for tiny doses

Rick Simpson Oil, or RSO, is a dark, tar-thick, full-extract cannabis oil that usually comes in a small oral syringe. RSO oil is strong: a VA research summary notes that THC in extracts such as oils and tinctures can reach 90%.

Do the math before you dose. A gram of oil at 70% THC holds about 700 mg of THC; compare that with the 10 mg limit on a Michigan adult-use edible serving. Measure RSO in tiny drops, expect it to act like an edible and let two full hours pass before you consider more. Read more on [what RSO is](/blog/what-is-rick-simpson-oil/) and [shopping for RSO](/blog/shopping-for-rso-guide/).

## Ratios on the label: CBD:THC and CBN blends

A ratio compares two cannabinoids, most often CBD and THC, so check which one the label lists first. A 20:1 CBD:THC product holds 20 times more CBD than THC, and 1:1 CBD:THC products hold equal milligrams of each. THC-forward products are the most likely to make you feel high. Think of the ratio as the balance; the milligrams per serving are the strength.

Some formulas add CBN and market it for evenings. A 2021 research review found the evidence on CBN dated and limited, too thin to support sleep claims. It also noted that these products usually contain 5 mg or less. See our [CBN explainer](/blog/what-is-cbn-benefits-effects/).

## Cannabis balm vs. lotion vs. tincture vs. RSO: comparison table

| Format | Onset | Duration | Dose control | Chance of a high (THC versions) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Balm or salve | Local, on the skin | Varies | Low | Low |
| Standard lotion | Local, on the skin | Varies | Low | Low |
| Transdermal patch or gel | Gradual | Steady release | Good | Yes |
| Tincture | Partly through the mouth, the rest like an edible | Outlasts inhaled cannabis | Good | Yes |
| RSO, swallowed | 30 minutes to 2 hours | Outlasts inhaled cannabis | Hard | Yes, even at small doses |

## How to choose a format, and what to ask

- **Want to avoid a high?** Choose a standard topical or a CBD-dominant product, and check the THC milligrams.
- **Want a measured dose?** A tincture's marked dropper gives the most control.
- **Experienced with edibles?** RSO is the most concentrated of these formats, so start smaller than you think.

Questions worth asking: What's the THC and CBD per serving and per package? Is it topical or transdermal? Which oils and fragrances are in it? At High Society, a budtender can help you read a label in store; health questions belong with your clinician. Cardholders can find more in our [patient guide](/patient-guide/). Recreational shoppers need to be 21 or older, while medical cardholders can buy from age 18. Enjoy cannabis responsibly.

faq.q: Will a THC lotion get me high?
faq.a: Usually not, if it's a standard topical. Cannabinoids tend to stay in the skin's outer layer, and a small study of THC salves found none in users' blood or urine after three days of use. Transdermal products are the exception: they're formulated to reach the bloodstream, so they can make you feel high.

faq.q: How is a balm different from a lotion?
faq.a: Texture and coverage. A balm or salve is thick and waxy, made for rubbing into one small area. A lotion contains more water, spreads easily and covers larger areas. Both are topicals that act on the skin, and neither is designed to reach the bloodstream unless it's labeled transdermal.

Start very small. RSO is highly concentrated, so check the label's THC per gram or per syringe and work out the milligrams in each drop. Take the smallest amount you can measure, then wait two hours or more before any second dose, since swallowed RSO acts like an edible. If you take medications, talk with your clinician first.

Sometimes, a little. Drops held under the tongue can absorb partly through the lining of the mouth, which may shorten the wait. In practice, much of a tincture gets swallowed, and that part acts like an edible, starting within 30 minutes to 2 hours. Hold off on a second serving until you know how the first one feels.

claims.claim: 'Wellness products' is a marketing label; these formats are chosen for practical reasons (no smoke, measured milligrams, a topical for one spot).
claims.source: editorial framing; no factual claim beyond the formats' descriptions

claims.claim: 'They haven't been shown to fix or relieve any medical condition' (body) and 'aren't proven to help any medical condition' (takeaway).
claims.fix: A sweeping negative: some cannabinoid medicines do have trial evidence, so the accurate statement is about these consumer formats. Reworded to 'None of them is an approved medicine, and research on these consumer formats is limited' (takeaway aligned).
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8612407/ (example of limited evidence for consumer claims); FDA approvals of cannabinoid medicines are general knowledge (Epidiolex, dronabinol, nabilone)

claims.claim: Cannabinoids are very fat-soluble; a review found CBD tends to collect in the skin's outer layer.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11172078/ (Lefebvre 2024, review-article: 'CBD's high lipophilicity ... it tends to accumulate in the SC instead of diffusing through other skin layers'; log P 6-7)

claims.claim: In one small German experiment, THC salves applied for three days left no detectable THC in three volunteers' blood or urine.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28122323/ (Hess 2017 abstract via Europe PMC: University of Bonn, Germany; 'three volunteers ... applied both types of salves over a period of 3days'; 'All of these blood and urine samples were tested negative for THC, 11-hydroxy-THC and 11-nor-9-carboxy-THC')

claims.claim: Transdermal patches, gels and lotions use carriers meant to move cannabinoids past the skin barrier into the bloodstream; the route can keep blood levels steady over hours.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11172078/ ('chemical penetration enhancers ... encapsulation in lipidic or polymeric delivery systems'; 'Transdermal delivery also ensures stable blood levels over an extended period')

claims.claim: In Michigan, non-oral THC products such as transdermal patches can hold up to 100 mg THC per dose.
claims.source: facts/law-facts.json mi-thc-limits (CRA technical bulletin Apr. 24, 2025: products not taken orally, 100 mg/dose); https://www.michigan.gov/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/bulletin/5Technical/Marihuana-Infused-Products-and-Edible-Marihuana-Product---Maximum-THC-limits-revised-42425.pdf (from law-facts, not re-opened)

claims.claim: Tinctures are sold 'with a dropper marked in milliliters'.
claims.fix: Not every tincture dropper is graduated. Reworded to 'a dropper that's often marked in milliliters'.
claims.source: general product knowledge

claims.claim: Under the tongue some THC absorbs through the mouth lining, but much is swallowed and acts like an edible.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11172078/ (sublingual placement; saliva production prompts swallowing, so the sublingual benefits are lost)

claims.claim: Swallowed cannabis takes effect within 30 minutes to 2 hours; full effects can take up to 4 hours.
claims.source: https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drugs-medication/cannabis/resources/lower-your-risks.html ('Effects felt within 30 minutes to 2 hours.' / 'It can take up to 4 hours to feel the full effects.')

claims.claim: Michigan adult-use tinctures: no more than 10 mg THC per dose and 200 mg per container.
claims.source: facts/law-facts.json mi-thc-limits (capsules, tinctures and oil drops: adult-use 10 mg/dose, 200 mg/container)

claims.claim: RSO is a dark, thick full-extract oil usually sold in an oral syringe.
claims.source: general product knowledge; no potency or health claim

claims.claim: THC in extracts such as oils and tinctures can reach 90% (VA research summary).
claims.source: https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/marijuana_ptsd_vets.asp ('The concentration of THC in these products can be as high as 90%.')

claims.claim: A gram of oil at 70% THC holds about 700 mg THC, versus the 10 mg Michigan adult-use edible serving limit.
claims.source: arithmetic (0.70 x 1,000 mg); facts/law-facts.json mi-thc-limits (adult-use edibles 10 mg/dose)

claims.claim: Ingested cannabis has a delayed onset and outlasts inhaled cannabis (table, RSO dosing advice).
claims.source: https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/marijuana_ptsd_vets.asp ('ingesting the same dose results in a delayed onset and longer duration of effect')

claims.claim: 'A ratio compares CBD to THC.'
claims.fix: Label conventions vary (some list THC first). Reworded: a ratio compares two cannabinoids, most often CBD and THC, so check which the label lists first; the 20:1 example now says CBD:THC.
claims.source: general label knowledge

claims.claim: A 2021 review found CBN evidence dated and limited, too thin for sleep claims; products marketed for sleep usually contain 5 mg or less.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8612407/ (Corroon 2021 abstract via Europe PMC, a review: 'dated and limited'; 'insufficient published evidence to support sleep-related claims'; 'cannabis products marketed for sleep (typically <=5 mg)')

review.notes: Independent fact-check 2026-10-24 (batch 9). Opened: Lefebvre 2024 (Europe PMC full text), Hess 2017 and Corroon 2021 (Europe PMC abstract records), the Health Canada page (WebFetch), the NCPTSD page (downloaded). The CRA bulletin is cited from facts/law-facts.json. All six sources exist, are https and support their sentences. Four claims fixed (five text edits): an over-broad negative health statement (body and takeaway), the dropper marking, ratio order on labels, and an unpublished staff promise.
review.writerNotes: Medical article: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links, no ordering section. Re-read and revised 2026-10-24: overlap-prone phrasings rewritten (edible onset, transdermal sentence, two-hour waits, the balm FAQ question), the budtender line no longer states a staff policy, and the secondary key phrases (balm vs lotion, THC tincture, RSO oil, CBD balm, transdermal cannabis lotion, 1:1 CBD THC products) are worked in. The primary key phrase uses "wellness", which docs/VOICE.md lists as a word High Society never uses; it appears only where the brief's key phrase needs it (H1, first paragraph, one heading), and the first paragraph frames it as a marketing label. The 70% / 700 mg RSO example is arithmetic on a hypothetical label, not a potency claim about any product. No claim that High Society carries balms, lotions, tinctures or RSO.
